explanations: terra: As Abraham and Ishmael raise the House's foundations, they voice a prayer for acceptance; physical raising, bodily work, and supplication occur together.

luna: The source section's root ذ ك ر moves between public honor and inward remembrance; this ayah gives remembrance a reciprocal form, commanding people to remember God with the promise that He will remember them. | terra: God commands people to remember Him and promises to remember them, making human dhikr and divinely granted mention reciprocal.

luna: The source section says its song sense resembles the camel-driver's chant; uncertainly, this ayah's image of someone calling to animals that hear only a call and shout (دُعَاءً وَنِدَاءً) marks what such a riding-call can sound like to its animal audience.

luna: The section names supplication as one sense of ذكر; here God says He is near and answers the supplicant when called (دَعْوَةَ الدَّاعِ إِذَا دَعَانِ), giving that prayerful address its own context. | terra: God is near and answers the caller's call; the inwardly directed supplication at the section's end does not require loudness in order to be heard.
terra: After the rites, people are to remember God as they remembered their forefathers or more intensely; divine dhikr redirects the public recitation of ancestral names.
terra: God raises some messengers above others in degrees; prophetic rank, rather than sound or mention, is the concrete object elevated here.

terra: The prayer asks God not to lay an iṣr upon the believers and not to make them carry what exceeds their capacity; divine removal of the Prophet's burden becomes a model for this requested relief.
terra: Zechariah calls upon his Lord for a good offspring while standing in this prayer setting; supplication gives the section's prayer-and-dua sense of dhikr an audible beginning.
terra: The angels call to Zechariah while he stands praying and announce Yahya by name; prayer is answered by a heard voice that raises a new name.
terra: Zechariah's sign is that he cannot speak to people except by gesture, yet he is told to remember his Lord much and glorify morning and evening; ordinary voice falls silent while dhikr remains.
terra: People remember God while standing, sitting, and lying on their sides; dhikr inhabits the body's changing positions rather than being only an abstract mental act.
terra: God desires to lighten people's load because the human being was created weak; it gives the bodily reason for divine easing without specifying an audible response.
terra: Once prayer is completed, believers are to remember God standing, sitting, and lying down; release from one act leads into embodied dhikr, closely paralleling فَإِذَا فَرَغْتَ فَٱنصَبْ.
terra: When the call to prayer is sounded, opponents take it as mockery and play; an audible act of worship is heard but denied its honor, reversing raised and honored dhikr.
terra: The Quran is revealed to the Prophet so that he warn his hearers and whoever it reaches, وَمَنۢ بَلَغَ; prophetic utterance is explicitly destined to travel beyond its first audience.

luna: The source section makes a back-bearing burden audible and then says it is lifted; this verse depicts wrongdoers carrying their burdens on their backs (أَوْزَارَهُمْ عَلَىٰ ظُهُورِهِمْ), a specific reverse in which the burden remains. | terra: The lost carry their burdens عَلَىٰ ظُهُورِهِمْ; this literal load-on-backs scene supplies the dark counterpart to the Prophet's burden being removed.

luna: The section ends with desire turned toward the Lord and remembrance held inwardly; this ayah describes people calling their Lord morning and evening, seeking His face (يَدْعُونَ رَبَّهُم بِالْغَدَاةِ وَالْعَشِيِّ يُرِيدُونَ وَجْهَهُ), a specific form of that orientation.
terra: No burden-bearing soul bears another's burden; this moral boundary clarifies that the Prophet's load in surah 94 is removed by God rather than transferred to another creature.

luna: The section turns the sound of zikr toward quiet supplication; this command says to call on one's Lord humbly and privately (تَضَرُّعًا وَخُفْيَةً), giving that inward register a direct form. | terra: The command to call the Lord humbly and secretly gives the supplication sense of dhikr a deliberately quiet vocal form.
terra: The Messenger removes people's burdens and shackles, reversing the direction of surah 94: the one whose own load was removed becomes the means by which others are unburdened.

luna: Before 7:205's inward remembrance below public loudness, this neighboring ayah commands listeners to hear the recitation and be silent (فَاسْتَمِعُوا لَهُ وَأَنصِتُوا), giving the section's ear a listening scene. | terra: When the Quran is recited, listeners are told to attend and be silent; it supplies the receptive silence immediately before 7:205's quiet inward remembrance.

luna: The source section's root ذ ك ر holds both elevated renown and remembrance within oneself; this ayah explicitly joins inward remembrance (فِي نَفْسِكَ) to prayerful fear and speech below public loudness (دُونَ الْجَهْرِ). | terra: The section explicitly makes this the inward pole of dhikr: the addressee remembers his Lord within himself, humbly and fearfully, دُونَ ٱلْجَهْرِ مِنَ ٱلْقَوْلِ, against the outwardly elevated sound of renown.
terra: The angels glorify their Lord and prostrate without pride, completing 7:205's inward remembrance with worshipful praise.

luna: The section's name and remembrance are sounds that reach a hearer; here hearts tremble when God is mentioned and faith increases when verses are recited (وَجِلَتْ قُلُوبُهُمْ), a specific bodily response to remembrance. | terra: Believers' hearts tremble when God is mentioned and their faith grows when His ayat are recited; heard sacred speech has a bodily resonance.

luna: The section names a fine caravan song and separately says ذكر can mean prayer and praise; this ayah sharply contrasts worship with whistling and handclapping (إِلَّا مُكَاءً وَتَصْدِيَةً), marking vocal noise as an empty substitute for prayer.
terra: A protected outsider is to be brought near until he hears God's word; recited revelation is presented as an audible message capable of reaching a new hearer.
terra: The Prophet's breast is constricted by what opponents say as he bears revelation; inward bodily pressure and the obligation to voice the message are held together.
terra: Joseph places the cup in his brother's saddlebag, رَحْلِ أَخِيهِ, and then a herald calls out to the caravan; saddle equipment and a projected human voice meet in the same ayah.
terra: The caravan turns toward the herald and answers his call, making the sound of 12:70 a two-sided exchange among travelers rather than an isolated shout.
terra: The herald's exchange offers a camel-load to whoever restores the missing cup, adding an explicitly named animal load to the caravan call begun in 12:70.

luna: The section ends with desire turning toward the Lord and inward remembrance; this ayah says hearts find rest in God's remembrance (بِذِكْرِ اللَّهِ تَطْمَئِنُّ الْقُلُوبُ), specifying the inward effect. | terra: Hearts find rest through remembrance of God, giving the inward bodily resolution of the section's movement away from a back strained by weight.
terra: A good word is likened to a sound tree whose branches reach the sky; speech is given the section's upward motion while remaining firmly rooted.
terra: The good-word tree continually gives fruit, extending 14:24's elevated utterance through time and showing how speech can remain productive after its first sound passes.
terra: A bad word is like an uprooted tree with no stability, reversing the raised, enduring good word of 14:24-25.
terra: Opponents address the Prophet as the recipient of the Reminder while calling him mad; their voiced insult tries to turn dhikr from honor into dishonor.
terra: The Prophet is commanded to proclaim openly what he has been ordered; this is the outward mission-voice whose renown must travel beyond a private utterance.
terra: God knows that the Prophet's breast is constricted by what opponents say; hostile speech is experienced as bodily pressure before the next ayah turns him to praise.
terra: The response to the constricted breast of 15:97 is to glorify the Lord's praise and prostrate, converting pressure caused by speech into prayer and praise.
terra: The sequence continues from constriction and praise into sustained worship, giving the section's فَٱنصَبْ the same movement from released burden into devotion.

luna: The section evokes a caravan's burdened backs and saddles; this ayah says riding animals carry people's loads to distant lands (تَحْمِلُ أَثْقَالَكُمْ إِلَىٰ بَلَدٍ), closely matching the loaded journey. | terra: Livestock carry people's loads to a land they could reach only with great bodily hardship; this is the Quran's clearest ordinary caravan scene behind the creaking saddle image.

luna: This ayah names horses, mules, and donkeys made for riding and adornment; neighboring 16:7 describes animals carrying loads to distant lands, giving the section's saddle and caravan song a specific riding scene.

terra: The command not to break, تَنقُضُوا, oaths after confirming them supplies the covenant-breaking branch of ن ق ض that 16:92 turns into visible unraveling; it marks how far the section's creaking sense stands from moral rupture.
terra: The woman who unravels her yarn after it was strong enacts the breaking branch of ن ق ض; it lets the creak named by the source lexicon hover at the edge of structural undoing.
terra: The repeated rule that no bearer bears another's burden preserves individual responsibility beside the exceptional divine act of lifting the Prophet's load.

luna: The section asks the reader to hear animal sound as part of its sound-world; this ayah says all things glorify God, though humans do not understand their glorification (لَا تَفْقَهُونَ تَسْبِيحَهُمْ), giving that sound a limit of intelligibility. | terra: Everything glorifies God's praise, though humans do not understand their glorification; the verse establishes meaningful nonhuman sound at the boundary of human hearing.

luna: The section's raised remembrance is meant to reach an ear; this ayah describes a covering over hearts and deafness in ears, then says that when the Lord alone is mentioned in the Quran, some turn away, a direct reversal of hearing. | terra: When the Prophet mentions his Lord alone in the Quran, opponents turn their backs in aversion; audible remembrance produces the bodily reverse of receptive listening.
terra: The Prophet is promised a praised station, مَقَامًا مَّحْمُودًا; it is a concrete form of elevated prophetic honor adjacent to the section's raised renown.

luna: The section hears words as sound and tracks what a listening ear receives; this ayah depicts people falling in prostration when the revealed verses are recited to them, a specific bodily response to voiced revelation.
luna: Those listeners answer the recitation in 17:107 by glorifying their Lord (سُبْحَانَ رَبِّنَا); this is a spoken praise following heard revelation, matching the section's sense of ذكر as praise.

luna: The listeners in 17:107 fall on their faces weeping and grow in humility; this ayah supplies the bodily response that completes the recitation scene, alongside the section's body-and-sound image.

luna: The section's remembrance includes prayer and a raised voice; here prayer is neither shouted nor wholly suppressed (وَلَا تَجْهَرْ بِصَلَاتِكَ وَلَا تُخَافِتْ بِهَا), but placed between the two. | terra: The Prophet is told neither to make his prayer loud nor wholly quiet but to seek a path between; this is the explicit vocal boundary between raised sound and inward remembrance.

luna: This repeated caller scene says people call their Lord morning and evening desiring His face; it contrasts them with someone whose heart is heedless of God's remembrance and follows desire, sharpening the section's turn from public renown to inward longing.
terra: Moses' companion says the journey has brought them نَصَبًا; travel fatigue supplies the Quranic caravan-side counterpart to the lexicon's nasb song sung along a road.

luna: The section turns from a name carried aloud to inward remembrance; Zakariya's prayer is described as a hidden call (نِدَاءً خَفِيًّا), directly staging supplication in a quiet voice. | terra: Zechariah calls his Lord نِدَآءً خَفِيًّا, a hidden or quiet call, a precise Quranic instance of supplication taking the inward sound-path described in the section.

luna: Zakariya says his bones have weakened (وَهَنَ الْعَظْمُ), a bodily counterpart to the strained back and ribs in the section; beside 19:3's hidden prayer, this weakness is voiced as a petition, though no creaking is stated. | terra: The quiet caller reports weakened bones and old age; an inward prayer emerges from a failing body, sharpening the section's attention to the sounds of joints and ribs.
terra: God answers Zechariah with good news of a son named Yahya, a name not previously given to another; the hidden call of 19:3 culminates in a uniquely uttered name.
terra: Zechariah is given a three-night inability to address people despite being sound; it establishes a bodily silence against which the next ayah's commanded praise is communicated.
terra: Unable to speak, Zechariah gestures to his people that they should glorify morning and evening, showing praise conveyed at the edge of audible voice.
terra: The command to mention Mary in the Book makes recited revelation a vehicle by which a human name is carried beyond its first time and place.
terra: The command to mention Abraham in the Book realizes his later truthful renown through repeated recitation of his name.

luna: This ayah says God gave the prophets a lofty, truthful tongue (لِسَانَ صِدْقٍ عَلِيًّا); it makes the section's raised remembrance as lasting honor concrete in the reputation granted among people. | terra: God gives Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob لِسَانَ صِدْقٍ عَلِيًّا, a lofty truthful tongue or renown, a direct Quranic image for a good name raised across distance and generations.
terra: Moses is to be mentioned in the Book as a chosen messenger and prophet, giving honorable remembrance a durable textual voice.
terra: Ishmael is to be mentioned in the Book and praised for fidelity, so named remembrance functions as the honor sense identified in the source section.
terra: The command to mention Idris in the Book preserves his name in recited scripture; the next ayah then distinguishes this textual remembrance from raising the prophet himself.
terra: God raises Idris to a high station, وَرَفَعْنَـٰهُ مَكَانًا عَلِيًّا; beside 19:56, it contrasts raising a prophet with raising a prophet's mention.
terra: The heavens nearly rupture, the earth splits, and mountains collapse under an asserted word; cosmic breaking amplifies the section's smaller creak of a body under pressure.
terra: This ayah identifies the pressure-producing claim in 19:90 as attributing a child to the Merciful, so a spoken proposition rather than a physical load causes the rupture.

luna: The section contrasts an elevated, heard name with inward remembrance; this ayah distinguishes speech spoken aloud from the secret and what is still more hidden (السِّرَّ وَأَخْفَى), giving the sound boundary a divine listener. | terra: Whether speech is made aloud or kept secret, God knows what is still more hidden; it preserves both ends of the section's audible-renown and inward-dhikr spectrum.

luna: The source section's dictionary gloss says ذكر includes prayer; this command explicitly pairs establishing prayer with remembrance of God (وَأَقِمِ الصَّلَاةَ لِذِكْرِي). | terra: God commands Moses to establish prayer لِذِكْرِى, making the section's dictionary statement that dhikr can be prayer explicit within an addressed prophetic command.
terra: Moses' prayer رَبِّ ٱشْرَحْ لِى صَدْرِى restages the opening bodily relief of surah 94 and begins a sequence that ends in speech, glorification, and remembrance.
terra: وَيَسِّرْ لِىٓ أَمْرِى asks for the task to be eased before the tongue is released, paralleling the movement from burden to ease and then to audible mission.
terra: Moses asks God to loosen the knot in his tongue; this gives the section's passage from bodily strain to prophetic sound another concrete bodily site.
terra: The purpose of the loosened tongue in 20:27 is that people understand قَوْلِى, making intelligible heard speech the outcome of bodily release.
terra: Moses asks that Aaron strengthen أَزْرِى, his supporting strength or back; it is a close bodily counterpart to the back that creaks under a load in the section.
terra: Moses asks that Aaron share his أَمْر, identifying the support of 20:31 as relief within the prophetic task rather than merely physical strength.
terra: The support requested in 20:29-32 is to enable abundant glorification, كَىْ نُسَبِّحَكَ كَثِيرًا, joining relief of strain to voiced praise.
terra: Moses adds وَنَذْكُرَكَ كَثِيرًا, so strengthened support and released speech culminate in the section's prayer-and-praise sense of dhikr.
terra: Whoever turns away from the revealed reminder given in 20:99 will carry a burden on resurrection; rejecting dhikr produces the very load that God removed from the Prophet.
terra: The burden of 20:100 is an abiding and evil load, حِمْلًا, completing the reversal between receiving remembrance and being crushed by weight.
terra: Voices are hushed before the Merciful until only a whisper is heard, supplying the low extreme against the section's sound that is raised and travels.
terra: The Prophet is told to bear patiently what opponents say and to glorify his Lord's praise at the day's edges; painful speech is answered by a disciplined sound of praise.

luna: The source section reads ذكر as honor and a name carried among people; this ayah calls the revealed Book a mention for its audience (فِيهِ ذِكْرُكُمْ), a distinct scriptural use that makes the honor/reminder sense explicit. | terra: The revealed book contains ذِكْرُكُمْ, which can be the addressees' reminder or their honor; that live ambiguity is the same remembrance-and-renown range the section hears in dhikr.

luna: In another account of David, mountains and birds glorify with him (يُسَبِّحْنَ مَعَ دَاوُودَ); this specifically joins the section's bird sounds to its dictionary sense of remembrance as praise. | terra: Mountains and birds are made to glorify with David; animal and landscape voices participate in the praise sense assigned to dhikr in the section.
terra: Job calls his Lord from bodily harm; like 38:41, the distressed body produces a Godward voice rather than remaining only an unarticulated groan.
terra: God answers Job and removes his harm, turning the burdened call of 21:83 into relief and making the event a remembrance for worshippers.
terra: Jonah calls from layered darkness with a confession and plea; an inward, hidden setting still carries a voice fully toward God.
terra: God responds to Jonah and saves him from distress, completing another movement from compressed suffering and prayer to release.
terra: The prophets call God رَغَبًا وَرَهَبًا, in hope and fear; the same desire-root as surah 94's فَٱرْغَبْ is realized here as prayer voiced toward God.
terra: God knows speech made aloud and what people conceal, restating the outward-and-inward vocal range in which the section places raised renown and hidden remembrance.

luna: The section evokes a caravan's finer riding-song and a name carried far; here Abraham is told to announce the pilgrimage (وَأَذِّنْ فِي النَّاسِ بِالْحَجِّ), after which people arrive on foot and lean camels from distant passes. | terra: Abraham is told to proclaim the pilgrimage to humanity, and the call brings riders on lean mounts from every distant pass; an elevated voice travels afar through the very caravan world evoked by the section's saddle-song.

luna: The pilgrims summoned in 22:27 are to mention God's name over the livestock provided for them (وَيَذْكُرُوا اسْمَ اللَّهِ); the ayah joins the section's traveling-animal scene to voiced remembrance in its own ritual context.
terra: Every community is given a rite so that God's name is mentioned over the livestock He provides; animal bodies and voiced remembrance are joined in worship.
terra: The humble are those whose hearts tremble when God is mentioned and who patiently bear what befalls them; voiced remembrance and endurance under affliction meet.

luna: The section's creaking saddle and animal sounds meet a ritual camel scene: over the camels standing in rows, people are commanded to mention God's name (فَاذْكُرُوا اسْمَ اللَّهِ عَلَيْهَا صَوَافَّ). | terra: God's name is to be mentioned over the sacrificial camels while they stand in rows; a human sacred utterance sounds over the large animals evoked by saddles and caravan song.

luna: The adjacent 22:36 names God over sacrificial camels; this ayah says their flesh and blood do not reach God, but piety does, a boundary that illuminates the section's shift from a publicly heard name to inward remembrance.

luna: This ayah places the two dictionary branches named in the section together: houses are permitted to be raised (تُرْفَعَ) and God's name mentioned and glorified in them (وَيُذْكَرَ فِيهَا اسْمُهُ). The raising is literal here, with voiced worship inside. | terra: Houses are permitted أَن تُرْفَعَ and God's name is remembered within them, وَيُذْكَرَ فِيهَا ٱسْمُهُ, bringing elevation and voiced remembrance into one scene.

luna: The section's 94:7–8 turn from completed work toward the Lord meets people whom trade does not distract from remembrance, prayer, and almsgiving (عَن ذِكْرِ اللَّهِ وَإِقَامِ الصَّلَاةِ); 24:36 supplies the neighboring setting of raised houses and praise. | terra: Within the raised houses of 24:36, people are not distracted from God's remembrance or prayer, so the elevated place becomes a sustained scene of dhikr rather than merely an architectural image.

luna: The section names eagle and chicken cries and then remembrance as prayer and praise; this ayah says birds and all in the heavens and earth know their prayer and glorification (تَسْبِيحَهُ), directly meeting animal voice with praise. | terra: Birds with wings outspread join all creation in prayer and glorification, each knowing its ṣalāh and tasbīḥ; animal sound meets precisely the prayer-and-praise branch of dhikr.
terra: Believers must not make the Messenger's calling among them like their calling of one another; the Prophet's call and name receive a distinct audible status.
terra: Moses says his breast constricts and his tongue does not move freely; the body under pressure is heard directly as difficulty in prophetic speech.

luna: The section reads ذِكر as honor carried beyond the moment; Abraham asks for a truthful tongue among later generations (لِسَانَ صِدْقٍ فِي الْآخِرِينَ), a prayer for a name that endures in people's speech. | terra: Abraham asks for لِسَانَ صِدْقٍ فِى ٱلْـَٔاخِرِينَ, truthful mention among later people; 19:50 answers the request and clarifies the enduring-voice sense of raised dhikr.
terra: The poets are followed by the erring; this begins a boundary around song-like speech that 26:227 will reopen only for poetry joined to faith, action, and abundant remembrance.
terra: Poets' wandering through every valley describes ungoverned imaginative speech, sharpening the controlled devotional exception in 26:227.
terra: Poets are faulted for saying what they do not do, so the decisive boundary is between sound alone and speech embodied in action.
terra: The exception among poets includes those who believe, act rightly, and remember God much; poetic voice and dhikr may meet, but only under an explicit ethical boundary.

luna: The section names bird and poultry cries as an animal branch of its sound image; Solomon says he was taught the speech of birds (مَنطِقَ الطَّيْرِ), a specific case where an animal voice carries intelligible speech. | terra: Solomon says that he and David were taught the speech of birds; the dictionary's eagle and chicken sounds become, in Quranic terms, an intelligible animal voice.

luna: An ant speaks and warns its community (قَالَتْ نَمْلَةٌ), and Solomon hears and smiles at her words; this gives the section's animal-sound detail a precise scene of a small creature's voice reaching a listener. | terra: An ant audibly warns its community of Solomon's approaching host; its small animal voice is the specific sound that Solomon hears and answers with prayer in 27:19.

luna: After hearing the ant in 27:18, Solomon turns to prayer, asking his Lord to enable gratitude (رَبِّ أَوْزِعْنِي أَنْ أَشْكُرَ); this joins the section's animal voice to its movement toward remembrance and praise. | terra: Solomon smiles at the ant's speech from 27:18 and immediately turns to a prayer of gratitude; heard animal voice becomes supplication directed to the Lord.
terra: The hoopoe speaks a report to Solomon, giving the bird-speech taught in 27:16 a concrete audible performance.
terra: God answers the distressed person when that person calls and removes the harm; the groan under pressure becomes an effective supplication and then relief.
terra: Moses calls Aaron more eloquent in tongue and asks that he be sent as vocal support, showing another person carrying part of a strained prophetic utterance.
terra: Disbelievers voice an offer to carry the sins of those who follow them; a spoken promise claims that another's burden can be taken up.
terra: They will in fact carry their own burdens and further burdens, exposing the false relief promised aloud in 29:12.
terra: Recitation of the Book, establishment of prayer, and remembrance of God are joined, and dhikr is called greater; it directly develops the section's prayer-and-praise sense of remembrance.

luna: The source section moves from animal cries to a finer camel-driver's song; this ayah names the donkey's voice as the most disagreeable sound (أَنْكَرَ الْأَصْوَاتِ لَصَوْتُ الْحَمِيرِ) and commands lowering one's voice, a specific boundary for animal sound. | terra: Luqman tells his son to lower his voice and names the donkey's voice as the harshest; voice height and an animal sound, two dictionary strands developed in the section, meet directly.

luna: The section ends with desire directed to the Lord; this ayah pictures people rising from their beds to call their Lord in fear and hope (يَدْعُونَ رَبَّهُمْ خَوْفًا وَطَمَعًا), giving that inward orientation a bodily and vocal setting. | terra: Their sides leave their beds as they call their Lord in fear and hope; bodily exertion, inward desire, and prayer converge as they do at the end of surah 94.
terra: Believers are commanded to remember God with abundant remembrance, giving dhikr the repeated communal voice that carries a name widely.
terra: The abundant remembrance of 33:41 is specified as glorification morning and evening, confirming its praise sense.
terra: God addresses the Prophet as witness, bearer of good news, and warner, roles enacted through the public voice whose reach the section hears in his raised mention.
terra: The Prophet is specifically a caller to God, دَاعِيًا إِلَى ٱللَّهِ, so his elevated public sound has the same Godward direction as the section's final inward desire.

luna: The section's ذكر includes prayer and praise, and its focus is the Prophet's raised mention; this ayah commands believers to bless and greet the Prophet (صَلُّوا عَلَيْهِ وَسَلِّمُوا), giving that honor a communal spoken form. | terra: God and the angels bless the Prophet and believers are commanded to voice blessings and peace upon him; his honored mention is repeatedly carried by other voices.
terra: The heavens, earth, and mountains recoil from bearing the Trust, while the human being bears it; a refused cosmic load sets the scale for bodily strain under a moral charge.

luna: The section's animal sound meets an explicit singing-like scene: mountains and birds are told to echo with David (أَوِّبِي مَعَهُ وَالطَّيْرَ), making animal voice a form of praise. | terra: Mountains and birds are commanded to echo or return praise with David; nonhuman sound becomes an answering song of glorification.

luna: The source section's root ر ف ع links elevation to voice and the honor of ذكر; this ayah says good speech rises to God (الْكَلِمُ الطَّيِّبُ يَصْعَدُ إِلَيْهِ), joining verbal sound to elevation while locating honor with God. | terra: Good speech ascends to God and righteous action يَرْفَعُهُ; spoken words literally take the upward path that the section hears in raised dhikr and desire directed to the Lord.

terra: A heavily laden soul calls out for help with its load, yet none of it is carried by another; the section's groan under weight becomes an explicit call, while divine relief in surah 94 reverses the refusal.
terra: The people of the lasting abode say that no نَصَب touches them there; this negated fatigue marks the final boundary of the exertion commanded by فَٱنصَبْ.

terra: God did not teach the Prophet poetry; his utterance is instead ذِكْرٌ and clear Quran. This directly guards the section's lexical nasb-song echo from collapsing prophetic remembrance into song.

luna: This ayah says Noah was left among later generations (وَتَرَكْنَا عَلَيْهِ فِي الْآخِرِينَ); that enduring remembrance is a concrete parallel to the section's honor carried beyond the moment. | terra: God leaves something enduring for Noah among later peoples; the following salutation shows that what remains is an honorable spoken remembrance.
terra: سَلَامٌ عَلَىٰ نُوحٍ فِى ٱلْعَـٰلَمِينَ voices Noah's name in peace throughout the worlds, completing the enduring mention of 37:78.

luna: This repeated legacy formula says Abraham was left among later generations (وَتَرَكْنَا عَلَيْهِ فِي الْآخِرِينَ), a specific instance of a name enduring in later people's memory. | terra: God leaves enduring mention for Abraham among later generations, answering Abraham's request in 26:84 for a truthful tongue after him.
terra: سَلَامٌ عَلَىٰٓ إِبْرَٰهِيمَ makes the enduring mention of 37:108 audible by pronouncing Abraham's name in blessing.

luna: This repeated legacy formula says Moses and Aaron were left among later generations (وَتَرَكْنَا عَلَيْهِمَا فِي الْآخِرِينَ), making the section's lasting honor recur for another pair of prophets. | terra: God leaves enduring mention for Moses and Aaron among later generations, another explicit form of prophetic renown made to outlast the body.
terra: سَلَامٌ عَلَىٰ مُوسَىٰ وَهَـٰرُونَ supplies the spoken names that complete the lasting remembrance announced in 37:119.

luna: This repeated legacy formula says Elijah was left among later generations (وَتَرَكْنَا عَلَيْهِ فِي الْآخِرِينَ), another concrete instance of remembrance outlasting the one remembered. | terra: God leaves enduring mention for Elias among later generations, repeating the Quranic pattern of preserving a prophet through praised speech.
terra: سَلَامٌ عَلَىٰٓ إِلْ يَاسِينَ voices the salutation that gives the enduring mention of 37:129 its audible form.

luna: This repeated David scene says the mountains echo praise with him at evening and sunrise (أَوِّبِي مَعَهُ); 38:19 names the assembled birds, completing the animal-voice scene in the next ayah. | terra: The mountains are subjected with David, glorifying at evening and sunrise; creation's sound is synchronized with a human prophet's praise.

luna: The birds assembled around David, each returning in praise (وَالطَّيْرَ مَحْشُورَةً), supply the animal voices adjacent to 38:18's mountains echoing with him. | terra: The gathered birds are each أَوَّابٌ with David, completing 38:18's chorus and giving the section's animal-sound branch a devotional direction.
terra: Job calls his Lord from bodily distress described as بِنُصْبٍ وَعَذَابٍ; this Quranic fatigue sense of ن ص ب meets both the section's straining body and its secondary song sense.
terra: No bearer bears another's burden, and all return to God; the boundary around human load-bearing directs final recourse to the same Lord desired in 94:8.

luna: The section links sound with bodily sensation; this ayah describes the revealed discourse making the skins of those who fear God shiver and then their skins and hearts soften at His remembrance (تَقْشَعِرُّ ... جُلُودُهُمْ), a concrete bodily response to recitation. | terra: At heard revelation, skins shiver and then skins and hearts soften toward ذِكْرِ ٱللَّهِ; remembrance becomes a sound registered inside the body, like the section's audible joints and ribs.
terra: When God alone is mentioned, some hearts recoil, while mention of others makes them rejoice; a heard name produces opposite bodily responses.
terra: The Prophet is told to persevere, seek forgiveness, and glorify his Lord's praise morning and evening; endurance and voiced devotion are again one response.
terra: God commands people to call upon Him and promises to answer; supplication is explicitly a directed voice whose destination guarantees its hearing.

luna: The section's sound carries a name to listeners; here opponents tell one another not to listen to the Quran and to make noise over it (وَالْغَوْا فِيهِ), a deliberate attempt to block hearing. | terra: Opponents tell one another not to listen to the Quran and to make noise over it; their deliberate din tries to cover the revealed voice, reversing the listening discipline of 49:2.
terra: The best speech belongs to one who calls to God and acts rightly; a voice gains elevation through its Godward direction and the deed accompanying it.

terra: The heavens nearly rupture above while the angels glorify their Lord's praise; structural breaking and a sound of praise occur together, closely matching the section's passage from creak to dhikr.

luna: The section brings a listener onto the sound of a creaking back and then remembrance; here riders settle on animals' backs (ظُهُورِهِ) and remember their Lord's favor (ذَكَرْتُمْ نِعْمَةَ رَبِّكُمْ), meeting the saddle scene with spoken gratitude. | terra: Once riders settle on the animals' backs, ظُهُورِهِ, they remember their Lord's favor and speak a praise; saddle, back, dhikr, and human voice meet in one act.

luna: The mounted riders' utterance in 43:13 ends by saying they will return to their Lord (إِنَّا إِلَىٰ رَبِّنَا لَمُنقَلِبُونَ); that return gives a voiced form to this section's final turn of longing toward the Lord. | terra: The riders' spoken praise in 43:13 ends by saying that they will return to their Lord, matching the section's turn of sound and desire toward God.

luna: The source section's root ذ ك ر spans remembrance and honor; this ayah calls the revealed message a reminder for the Prophet and his people (لَذِكْرٌ لَّكَ وَلِقَوْمِكَ), then says they will be questioned about it. | terra: The Quran is called a ذِكْرٌ for the Prophet and his people, plausibly both reminder and honor for which they will answer, directly activating the section's paired senses.
terra: A group of jinn attend the Prophet while he recites the Quran and tell one another to listen; his otherwise human voice reaches an unseen audience.
terra: After hearing the recitation, the jinn name it a revealed book and carry its guidance onward, extending the first heard voice through new speakers.
terra: Believers are commanded to support and honor the Messenger and to glorify God morning and evening; prophetic honor and spoken praise are coordinated in one command.

luna: The source section hears 94:4's raised remembrance as a voice reaching listeners; this ayah sets the boundary directly: believers must not raise their voices above the Prophet's voice (لَا تَرْفَعُوا أَصْوَاتَكُمْ فَوْقَ صَوْتِ النَّبِيِّ). | terra: The section explicitly sets this command beside raised prophetic renown: believers must not let their own أَصْوَاتَكُمْ rise above صَوْتِ ٱلنَّبِىِّ, so the root ر ف ع becomes a boundary around the Prophet's audible voice.

luna: The next ayah gives the converse sound: voices are lowered in the Prophet's presence (وَاغْضُضْ مِنْ أَصْوَاتِكُمْ), making audible reverence the limit of the section's raised-name image. | terra: Those who lower their voices before the Messenger are praised, giving the positive form of the vocal limit stated in 49:2.

luna: The section asks the reader to hear the Prophet's name; this passage depicts people calling him from behind the chambers (يُنَادُونَكَ مِن وَرَاءِ الْحُجُرَاتِ), the same vocal setting as 49:2's rule on voices. | terra: People call the Prophet from behind his chambers; the ayah censures a loud mode of reaching him and shows that not every extension of his name honors him.

luna: The callers in 49:4 are told that waiting until the Prophet comes out would be better for them; this ayah completes the boundary between clamorous calling and respectful address beside 49:2's voice instruction. | terra: Waiting silently until the Prophet comes out would be better than the calls of 49:4, making restraint itself part of the scene's proper treatment of voice.
terra: God knows what the soul whispers within and is nearer than the jugular vein; this is the bodily interior limit of the section's inward remembrance.

luna: The section asks a reader to hear the raised remembrance; this ayah calls the reminder useful to one who has a heart or lends an ear (وَأَلْقَى السَّمْعَ وَهُوَ شَهِيدٌ), specifying receptive listening.
terra: The Prophet is commanded to endure what people say and glorify his Lord's praise before sunrise and sunset, repeating the passage from oppressive speech to dhikr.
terra: The praise commanded in 50:39 continues through part of the night and after prostration, sustaining the Godward voice after the day's hostile words have ended.
terra: The Prophet is told to continue reminding, and the ayah clears him of being a soothsayer or mad; the next ayah adds the accusation of poetry.
terra: Opponents call the reminding Prophet a poet, illustrating the very confusion between revealed dhikr and song-like utterance that 36:69 rejects.
terra: While patiently awaiting God's judgment, the Prophet is told that he is under divine care and to glorify his Lord's praise when he rises; bodily rising becomes praise after strain.
terra: The glorification of 52:48 continues at night and as the stars withdraw, extending praise into the quietest hours.
terra: The Prophet does not speak from personal desire; this distinguishes the authority of his audible speech from ordinary human voices that 49:2 must not place over it.
terra: His utterance is identified as revelation conveyed to him, completing 53:3 and explaining why the prophetic voice bears exceptional weight and honor.
terra: The scrolls of Moses and Abraham state that no burden-bearer bears another's burden, making non-transfer a remembered ancient rule against which divine relief stands out.
terra: Hearts are called to become humble at God's remembrance and revealed truth; dhikr is heard deeply enough to alter the body within.
terra: God has heard the woman arguing with the Prophet and complaining to Him and hears their dialogue; a burden voiced toward God is heard even without any suggestion of public loudness.
terra: God raises believers and people of knowledge by degrees; it supplies an honor-elevation sense of ر ف ع alongside the section's elevation of a prophet's mention and voice.
terra: Were the Quran laid upon a mountain, it would be seen humbled and cracked from fear; the word itself becomes a load that makes a body-like structure break under strain.
terra: Jesus announces a messenger to come after him whose name is أَحْمَدُ, staging the Prophet's name as a sound sent ahead of him through time.

luna: The section names the creaking of saddles and howdahs; this ayah pictures a donkey carrying books (الْحِمَارِ يَحْمِلُ أَسْفَارًا), a specific loaded-animal counterpart to that traveling gear. | terra: The Torah-bearer who does not bear its meaning is likened to a donkey carrying books; the laden animal gives the saddle-and-load scene a warning about carrying words without inward remembrance.

luna: The section describes remembrance as prayer and as sound; here the call to Friday prayer (نُودِيَ لِلصَّلَاةِ) is followed by a command to hasten to God's remembrance (فَاسْعَوْا إِلَىٰ ذِكْرِ اللَّهِ), explicitly joining call and dhikr. | terra: The public call to Friday prayer summons believers to ذِكْرِ ٱللَّهِ, making dhikr at once an audible summons and the worship toward which it calls.

luna: After prayer, people disperse, seek God's bounty, and remember Him much (وَاذْكُرُوا اللَّهَ كَثِيرًا); this gives a concrete parallel to the section's sequence of finishing one task and turning toward the Lord, following 62:9's call. | terra: After the prayer is finished, believers disperse, seek God's bounty, and remember Him much; the after-completion structure directly illuminates the renewed exertion of 94:7.

luna: The section's raised and inward registers meet this statement that God knows speech kept secret or spoken aloud (أَسِرُّوا قَوْلَكُمْ أَوِ اجْهَرُوا بِهِ), while the ayah locates that speech's knowledge in hearts. | terra: Whether people conceal their speech or make it public, God knows what breasts contain; inward and outward sound are held within one divine hearing.
terra: The Prophet is warned not to be like Jonah when he called out while choked with distress; the ayah remembers suffering through the voice it forced from him.
terra: When disbelievers hear the Reminder, they nearly make the Prophet slip with their looks and call him mad; audible dhikr provokes an attack on the very honor God raises.
terra: The utterance heard in 68:51 is affirmed as a remembrance for all worlds, extending its range far beyond the hostile first hearers.
terra: The revelation is called the speech of a noble messenger, setting up the next ayah's denial that this elevated utterance is a poet's performance.
terra: The messenger's utterance is not the word of a poet; like 36:69, this draws a firm boundary between revealed dhikr and the section's secondary song sense of nasb.
terra: After the passage distinguishes revelation from a poet's speech, the Prophet is commanded to glorify the name of his Lord; revealed utterance ends in voiced praise rather than song.
terra: The jinn report that they heard a wondrous Quran, another scene in which the Prophet's recitation travels beyond the visible human audience.

luna: The section compares a fine riding song with remembrance and prayer; this command to recite the Quran in measured recitation (وَرَتِّلِ الْقُرْآنَ تَرْتِيلًا) gives a specific, deliberate mode of voiced sacred words. | terra: The Prophet is told to recite the Quran in measured recitation; this gives the weighty word of 73:5 its disciplined audible form.
terra: God will cast upon the Prophet قَوْلًا ثَقِيلًا, a weighty word; the revelation is simultaneously speech and a load capable of making a prophetic body strain.
terra: Night rising is described as stronger in bodily impression and more upright in speech, أَقْوَمُ قِيلًا, joining exertion under weight to the formation of a sound.

luna: The section's final desire is directed to the Lord, and it names ذكر as spoken remembrance; this command says to remember the Lord's name and devote oneself wholly to Him (وَتَبَتَّلْ إِلَيْهِ تَبْتِيلًا). | terra: وَٱذْكُرِ ٱسْمَ رَبِّكَ وَتَبَتَّلْ إِلَيْهِ makes remembrance of the Lord's name turn wholly toward Him, matching the section's inward turn at surah 94's close.
terra: The enwrapped Prophet is told to rise and warn, turning bodily rising into the public voice of his mission.
terra: Immediately after rising to warn, he is told to magnify his Lord; proclamation turns into praise, as the section's outward and Godward sound paths do.

luna: The source section's dictionary account of root ن ق ض names sounds of fingers and joints; this ayah singles out fingertips (بَنَانَهُ) as bodily detail God can reassemble, though it does not itself describe a sound.
terra: The Prophet is told not to move his tongue hurriedly with the revelation; a small bodily motion is the threshold at which the Quran becomes audible in his voice.
terra: God assumes responsibility for gathering the revelation and its recitation, placing the weight of forming the utterance beyond the Prophet's straining tongue.
terra: Once God has recited the revelation, the Prophet is to follow its recitation; his voice follows a sound first given to him.
terra: The Prophet is commanded to remain patient under his Lord's judgment and not obey sinners; it names the pressure from which 76:25 turns to remembered speech.
terra: After the command to patience in 76:24, the Prophet is told to remember his Lord's name morning and evening, moving from pressure to repeated named remembrance.
terra: Prostration and long nightly glorification continue the named remembrance of 76:25 into bodily worship.

luna: The source section uses ذكر for voiced honor and prayer; this ayah calls the revelation a reminder (تَذْكِرَةٌ), the written/revealed sense of the same source root, distinct from the section's audible reputation.

luna: This ayah places the revelation in honored sheets (فِي صُحُفٍ مُّكَرَّمَةٍ); neighboring 80:14 says they are raised and purified, giving the section's raised remembrance a material written counterpart.

luna: The reminder named in 80:11 is described here as elevated and purified (مَرْفُوعَةٍ مُّطَهَّرَةٍ); neighboring 80:13 identifies the honored sheets, giving a physical counterpart to the section's raised ذكر rather than the same vocal scene. | terra: The reminder is in scrolls described as raised and purified; written revelation itself receives the elevation that the section gives to remembered speech.
terra: The sky splits open, enlarging the section's creaking body into a structure that actually breaks under the final summons.
terra: The split sky heeds or listens to its Lord and fulfills its due; structural breaking is paired with receptive hearing and Godward obedience.
terra: Humanity labors toward its Lord with strenuous labor and will meet Him; the exertion of فَٱنصَبْ and the direction of فَٱرْغَبْ are fused in one Godward movement.

luna: The section joins remembrance, praise, and elevation; this command explicitly says to glorify the name of the Lord Most High (سَبِّحِ اسْمَ رَبِّكَ الْأَعْلَىٰ), a close meeting of name, praise, and height. | terra: The command to glorify the name of the Lord Most High fuses praise, a spoken name, and height in one formulation.
terra: God promises to make the Prophet recite so that he will not forget; the enduring revelation is carried through a divinely secured prophetic voice.

luna: The source section's dictionary sense of ذكر includes prayer and praise; this ayah says the successful person remembers the Lord's name and prays (وَذَكَرَ اسْمَ رَبِّهِ فَصَلَّىٰ), joining those acts in sequence. | terra: The successful person remembers the name of his Lord and then prays, فَصَلَّىٰ, placing named remembrance and ṣalāh in the same compact sequence.
terra: Faces in the Fire are عَامِلَةٌ نَّاصِبَةٌ, laboring and exhausted; the same root turns devoted exertion into futile, punishing toil.

luna: The section hears a name raised through speech; this command to proclaim the Lord's favor (فَحَدِّثْ) makes speaking what was received a specific counterpart to an elevated remembrance. | terra: The Prophet is told to proclaim his Lord's favor, فَحَدِّثْ, turning received relief into an audible account immediately before surah 94's burden-and-renown sequence.
terra: The first command to recite is explicitly in the name of the Lord, joining prophetic voice and named remembrance at their source.
terra: In response to divine abundance, the Prophet is told to pray to his Lord and sacrifice; received relief or gift leads directly into worship, as at the close of surah 94.
terra: The Prophet's hater is the one cut off, reversing the raised and enduring prophetic mention: hostility passes while the honored name remains.
terra: After the promised opening and people entering the faith, the Prophet is commanded to glorify his Lord's praise; completed work turns into voiced devotion just as in 94:7-8.
